bible_refs.note: κυριεύειν … τοῦ ἀνθρώπου τὸν νόμον ἐφ' ὅσον χρόνον ζῇ, reported speech of Romans 7:1.
ἐσταύρωται μὲν αὐτὸς τῷ κόσμῳ, καὶ μὴν ὁ κόσμος αὐτῷ echoes Galatians 6:14 ἐμοὶ κόσμος ἐσταύρωται κἀγὼ κόσμῳ.
Lemma repeated three times; the second half (οὐ γὰρ ὃ θέλω τοῦτο πράσσω, ἀλλ' ὃ μισῶ τοῦτο ποιῶ) once.
Cyril's order: οἱ τὰ ἐπίγεια φρονοῦντες, ὧν ὁ θεὸς ἡ κοιλία, καὶ ἡ δόξα ἐν τῇ αἰσχύνῃ αὐτῶν; the NT has the participle clause last. Translated in Cyril's order.
LXX Joel 1:5 ἐκνήψατε, οἱ μεθύοντες ἐξ οἴνου αὐτῶν; same verse number in Hebrew/English versification.

choices.english: the One who knows all things
choices.why: ὁ πάντα εἰδώς ('the One who knows all things') is God; capitalized 'One'.

γράφεται (middle) is the legal term 'to indict'; rendered 'brings a charge against'. τὸ πρόσωπον … περιτιθείς = 'taking on himself the part (role)', Cyril's reading that Paul speaks in the person of the weak, not of himself.
ἐξιτηλία ('fading, transience') rendered 'the fleeting things'; no extra noun such as 'pleasures' added.
παρακεκομμένοι (literally 'debased, counterfeited') rendered 'impaired' for the mind's lost precision (τὸ ἀκριβές).

βραβεύοντα and παιδαγωγοῦντα are accusative and agree with τὸν … ζυγόν, so the yoke of the law (not God, who is nominative ὁ πάντα εἰδώς) is what directs and trains; τὸ αὐτῷ δοκοῦν is 'what pleases him' (God). The tutoring image recalls the law as παιδαγωγός (Galatians 3:24) but is not a quotation, so it is not cited inline.

pass_a_gloss: [continuing u05-open: not even] would the one who knows all (ὁ πάντα εἰδώς) have laid on (ἐπετίθει) us the yoke (ζυγός) from the law, arbitrating (βραβεύοντα) very well what seems good to him and tutoring (παιδαγωγοῦντα) toward what is profitable, if he knew us caught in the nooses of fate? Either let the opponents say that God did not know this, or if, having chosen to think rightly, they greatly fear to pour ignorance over the unspeakable glory—and they say he has legislated (νενομοθετηκέναι), and will confess plainly that he fixed the penalties of wrongdoers—he surely knows man living with a free mind and able to dart with willing inclinations toward whatever he wishes, nothing hindering. Therefore the inspired Paul said the law is lord over man as long as he lives; so not as if the human understanding were subject to others' nods does he say such things; but he reasons as a philosopher and examines the passions of human nature, and all but digs out subtly the inner sicknesses toward the mind, and indicts the body for inborn love of pleasure, putting round himself the person of one still sick (νοσοῦντος) with love of the flesh. For though he was crucified (ἐσταύρωται) to the world and the world to him, and was truly admirable, he thought it wise not to look at his own gift of grace but to make the weakness of those not yet become like him a necessary subject for his discourse. So when you hear him say, What I work I do not know, think of some exceedingly (ὑπεράγαν) sinful people who think they live the best of lives and that nothing could equal the luxury and fleetingness in this world; for they loathe the ways of decency, but pride themselves and luxuriate in their own pleasures; and about them, I think, Paul says: those minding earthly things, whose god is the belly, and the glory in their shame. These might fittingly say, fulfilling what is base as something highly praised: What I work I do not know. So let them hear: sober up, drunkards, from their wine. pass_b_english: … would the One who knows all things have laid on us the yoke of the law, which so well directs what pleases him and trains us toward what is profitable, if he had known that we were caught in the nooses of Fate? Either let our opponents say that God did not know this; or, if they have chosen to think rightly and are deeply afraid to pour ignorance over his ineffable glory, they say that he gave laws, and indeed they will plainly confess that he fixed the penalties for wrongdoers. Then surely he knows that man lives with a free mind and is able to move by voluntary inclination toward whatever he wishes, with nothing to hinder him.

That is why the inspired Paul said that the law has dominion over a person for as long as he lives (Romans 7:1). He does not say such things, then, as though the human mind were subject to the nod of others. Rather, he reasons as a philosopher and examines closely the passions of human nature. He all but digs out with precision the sicknesses that reach inward to the mind, and he brings a charge against the body for its inborn love of pleasure, very fittingly taking on himself the part of one who is still sick with love of the flesh.

For though he himself had been crucified to the world, and the world to him (Galatians 6:14), and was truly worthy of admiration, he still thought it wise not to look to his own gift, but to make the weakness of those not yet like him the necessary subject of his discourse.

So when you hear him say, “For what I am doing, I do not understand” (Romans 7:15), think of certain exceedingly great sinners who suppose that they are living the truly best life, and that nothing could equal the luxury and the fleeting things of this world. They loathe the ways of decency, but they take pride in their own pleasures and wallow in them without restraint. It is of them, I think, that Paul says, “Those who set their minds on earthly things, whose god is the belly, and whose glory is in their shame” (Philippians 3:19). These people, carrying out what is base as though it were something highly praised, might fittingly say, “For what I am doing, I do not understand.”

Let them hear, then: “Wake up, you drunkards, from your wine” (Joel 1:5). For just as lovers of drink and the drunken, their clear thinking impaired by the passion, would not know what they were doing while they were drunk, so those whose minds have grown sick from love of the flesh and the most shameful pleasures would not know what they are doing at all. So Paul is explaining to us a disease of the human heart when he says, “For what I am doing, I do not understand.”

But suppose there is someone who offers a tenderer heart, as it were, to the reproofs of conscience, who is grieved that he does wrong, yet is still overpowered by the pleasures that lead to sin, and goes toward wrongdoing as if against his will. He might fittingly say, “For I do not practice what I want, but I do what I hate” (Romans 7:15). Rest of the section checked clause by clause against the Greek and kept; Romans 7:1, Galatians 6:14, Romans 7:15, Philippians 3:19 and Joel 1:5 (LXX, same numbering) verified.
